The White-breasted robin (Eopsaltria georgiana) is a small passerine endemic to the jarrah and karri forests of southwestern Australia. Eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after a period of 14 days [ab = 14 days], an incubation duration that aligns closely with that of other Australo-Papuan robins of the family Petroicidae weighing under 20 grams. Newly hatched nestlings emerge with a wet weight of approximately 2.0 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.0 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the altricial condition typical of this clade. The subsequent growth trajectory is rapid, fueled by intensive biparental provisioning of arthropod prey. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of the active metabolic period in this species (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), a predictable sequence of post-hatching milestones occurs. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest, takes place 13.5 days after hatching [tx = 13.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively short nestling period is consistent with the high predation pressure typical of Mediterranean-climate ecosystems, where forest mortality on nests is substantial.

Gonadal maturation in this species proceeds gradually during the post-fledging and juvenile stages. Under the same thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that governs active metabolic processes, individuals attain sexual maturity at 40.5 days after hatching [tp = 40.5 days after hatching]. This relatively early onset of reproductive capacity, compared to the overall lifespan, suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward rapid turnover in a seasonally predictable environment. Following puberty, young birds typically delay their first breeding attempt until they have secured a territory and formed a stable pair bond. Field records indicate that the first successful brood is initiated 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], meaning that first-year birds generally do not breed during their first spring but wait until the subsequent breeding season at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This deferral of first reproduction likely reflects the time required to acquire a high-quality territory in the dense understory habitat and to develop the foraging efficiency necessary to sustain a clutch. The interval between attaining sexual maturity and first breeding thus represents a critical period of resource acquisition and social integration.

Female White-breasted robins ultimately reach an adult body mass of 17.5 grams [Wwi = 17.5 grams], while males attain a slightly larger ultimate wet weight of 20.8 grams [Wwi = 20.8 grams]. This modest sexual size dimorphism, with males approximately 19% heavier than females, is unusual among Petroicidae and may be linked to the species' territorial system, in which males engage in vigorous song displays and physical defense of resources. The initial wet weight of a newly laid egg is 2.50 grams [Ww0 = 2.50 grams], representing a substantial maternal investment relative to adult female mass. This egg mass, roughly 14% of the female's body mass, is among the higher relative egg sizes recorded for the genus, and it likely contributes to the relatively well-developed state of the hatchling. Comparisons with congeners such as the Eastern yellow robin suggest that the comparatively large egg size in E. georgiana may facilitate a shorter nestling period, thereby reducing cumulative exposure to nest predation during the brooding phase.

Reproductive output in Eopsaltria georgiana is structured around a consistent pattern of two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], a figure that is invariant across most of the species' geographic range. Breeding pairs typically produce two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], timed to coincide with the peak arthropod abundance that follows late winter and spring rains. The total annual reproductive output is therefore four eggs per breeding female per annum, a modest but reliable figure that contrasts with the higher fecundity observed in many northern temperate passerines. This two-clutch strategy appears to be constrained by the length of the favorable breeding season in the Mediterranean-climate zone, where summer drought sharply reduces prey availability for provisioning nestlings. Pairs that initiate a first clutch early in the season, in late August, are more likely to complete a successful second brood before the onset of the dry summer period, suggesting that phenological timing strongly influences annual productivity.

Maximum recorded longevity for the White-breasted robin in the wild is seven years [am = seven years], based on banding returns from long-term population studies in the Dryandra Woodland re at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]gion. This lifespan, when considered against the species' moderately paced reproductive schedule, yields a life-history profile characteristic of a small passerine occupying a relatively stable but resource-limited environment. The combination of a seven-year lifespan (7 years) [am = 7 years], deferred first reproduction at one year, and modest annual productivity of four eggs translates into a relatively low lifetime reproductive output compared to many similarly sized northern hemisphere songbirds at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. However, adult survival appears to be high, with annual apparent survival rates exceeding 60% in undisturbed habitat, which offsets the modest fecundity. This demographic pattern aligns with the broader syndrome observed in the Australo-Papuan avifauna, where stable, year-round residency in aseasonal or mildly seasonal environments favors investment in adult survival over high annual fecundity, a contrast to the boom-and-bust strategies of migratory temperate passerines.
